steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the Methodology section of the encyclopedia article on algorithm engineering, covering its cycle of design, analysis, implementation and experiments, plus applications and algorithm libraries.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Some researchers see the methodology of algorithm engineering as a cycle. The cycle consists of algorithm design, analysis, implementation and experimental evaluation, and there are further aspects added to it like machine models or realistic inputs.

They think it is too limited to say algorithm engineering is the same as experimental algorithmics. If design and analysis, implementation and experimentation are seen as separate activities, then the crucial feedback loop between these elements of algorithm engineering is ignored.

### Realistic models and real inputs

Specific applications are not part of the methodology of algorithm engineering, but they still play an important role. They shape realistic models of the problem and of the underlying machine, and they supply real inputs and other design parameters for the experiments.

### Design

Algorithm theory usually focuses on the asymptotic behavior of algorithms. Algorithm engineers have to keep more requirements in mind than that: the algorithm should be simple, it should be implementable in programming languages on real hardware, and it should allow code reuse.

Also, the constant factors of algorithms have a big impact on real-world inputs. The impact is so big that sometimes an algorithm with worse asymptotic behavior is better in practice, because its constant factors are lower.

### Analysis

Some problems can be solved in a simpler and more efficient way with heuristics and randomized algorithms than with deterministic algorithms. The problem is that this makes even simple randomized algorithms hard to analyze, because there are subtle dependencies that have to be taken into account.

- Implementation
  - huge semantic gaps: theoretical insights / formulated algorithms / programming languages / hardware
  - small implementation details -> rippling effects on execution behavior
  - only reliable way to compare implementations: lots of tuning and profiling, multiple architectures, look at generated machine code
- Experiments
  - see Experimental algorithmics
- Application engineering
  - experiment code differs from application code
  - experiments: fast prototyping, performance, instrumentation for measurements
  - applications: thorough testing, maintainability, simplicity, tuning for particular input classes
- Algorithm libraries
  - stable, well-tested libraries e.g. LEDA -> technology transfer, faster adoption of new algorithms
  - reduce investment and risk for practitioners: no need to understand and implement academic results themselves

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Some researchers see the methodology of algorithm engineering as a cycle. The cycle consists of algorithm design, analysis, implementation and experimental evaluation, and there are further aspects added to it like machine models or realistic inputs.

They think it is too limited to say algorithm engineering is the same as experimental algorithmics. If design and analysis, implementation and experimentation are seen as separate activities, then the crucial feedback loop between these elements of algorithm engineering is ignored.

### Realistic models and real inputs

Specific applications are not part of the methodology of algorithm engineering, but they still play an important role. They shape realistic models of the problem and of the underlying machine, and they supply real inputs and other design parameters for the experiments.

### Design

Algorithm theory usually focuses on the asymptotic behavior of algorithms. Algorithm engineers have to keep more requirements in mind than that: the algorithm should be simple, it should be implementable in programming languages on real hardware, and it should allow code reuse.

Also, the constant factors of algorithms have a big impact on real-world inputs. The impact is so big that sometimes an algorithm with worse asymptotic behavior is better in practice, because its constant factors are lower.

### Analysis

Some problems can be solved in a simpler and more efficient way with heuristics and randomized algorithms than with deterministic algorithms. The problem is that this makes even simple randomized algorithms hard to analyze, because there are subtle dependencies that have to be taken into account.

### Implementation

There are huge semantic gaps between theoretical insights, formulated algorithms, programming languages and hardware. These gaps make efficient implementations of even simple algorithms a challenge, since small implementation details can have rippling effects on how the code executes.

The only reliable way to compare several implementations of an algorithm is to spend a lot of time on tuning and profiling, to run the algorithms on multiple architectures, and to look at the machine code that is generated.

### Experiments

See: Experimental algorithmics

### Application engineering

The implementations of algorithms that are used for experiments are different in significant ways from code that can be used in applications.

Experiment code puts fast prototyping, performance and instrumentation for measurements first, while application code needs thorough testing, maintainability, simplicity, and tuning for particular classes of inputs.

### Algorithm libraries

Algorithm libraries that are stable and well tested, like LEDA, play an important role in technology transfer, because they speed up how fast new algorithms are adopted in applications.

These libraries reduce the investment and risk for practitioners, since practitioners no longer have to understand and implement the results of academic research themselves.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Some researchers describe the methodology of algorithm engineering as a cycle of algorithm design, analysis, implementation and experimental evaluation, joined by further aspects such as machine models or realistic inputs.

They argue that equating algorithm engineering with experimental algorithmics is too limited, because treating design and analysis, implementation and experimentation as separate activities ignores the crucial feedback loop between these elements of algorithm engineering.[1]

### Realistic models and real inputs

Although specific applications lie outside the methodology of algorithm engineering, they play an important role in shaping realistic models of the problem and the underlying machine, and they supply real inputs and other design parameters for experiments.[1]

### Design

Algorithm theory usually focuses on the asymptotic behavior of algorithms, but algorithm engineers need to keep further requirements in mind: simplicity of the algorithm, implementability in programming languages on real hardware, and allowing code reuse.

In addition, constant factors of algorithms have such a considerable impact on real-world inputs that an algorithm with worse asymptotic behavior sometimes performs better in practice because of lower constant factors.

### Analysis

Some problems can be solved more simply and efficiently with heuristics and randomized algorithms than with deterministic algorithms. Unfortunately, this makes even simple randomized algorithms difficult to analyze, as there are subtle dependencies to take into account.[1]

### Implementation

Huge semantic gaps between theoretical insights, formulated algorithms, programming languages and hardware make efficient implementations of even simple algorithms a challenge, because small implementation details can have rippling effects on execution behavior.

The only reliable way to compare several implementations of an algorithm is to spend a considerable amount of time on tuning and profiling, run the algorithms on multiple architectures, and look at the generated machine code.[1]

### Experiments

See: Experimental algorithmics

### Application engineering

Implementations of algorithms used for experiments differ significantly from code that is usable in applications.

The former prioritizes fast prototyping, performance and instrumentation for measurements during experiments, whereas the latter requires thorough testing, maintainability, simplicity, and tuning for particular classes of inputs.[1]

### Algorithm libraries

Stable, well-tested algorithm libraries such as LEDA play an important role in technology transfer by speeding up the adoption of new algorithms in applications.

Such libraries reduce the investment and risk required of practitioners, because they remove the burden of understanding and implementing the results of academic research.

References:
[1] "Algorithm Engineering – An Attempt at a Definition", Peter Sanders, web: http://algo2.iti.kit.edu/documents/definition.pdf
